title: The Wrong Smile
premise: Ivo Pemberton, a property surveyor who has built her whole life on the belief that nothing is real unless it can be measured, arrives at Hollowmere House to appraise it for a grieving family and finds her childhood imaginary friend, Wren, waiting on the porch exactly as she left him twenty-five years ago. Wren warns that the house counts its residents, and when the count reaches a number Ivo can't yet name, the family will be folded into its walls like the previous owners before them. As Ivo's professional skepticism wars with mounting evidence—the rooms that measure larger inside than out, the surveyor's instruments that return her own handwriting—she must decide whether loyalty to her own disbelief is worth more than the truth that could save the Delacorte family. In the end, Ivo sacrifices her invisibility, letting the house count her instead, and walks Wren out the front door as the walls close behind her, finally seen, finally believed, and finally gone.
about_author: Ulyana Villalobos is a former building inspector from coastal Maine who spent eleven years crawling through other people's basements before turning to horror fiction. She writes about the quiet dread of old houses and the people who refuse to listen to them.

chapters.title: The Commission
chapters.summary: Ivo Pemberton, POV. Ivo takes the Hollowmere House appraisal job partly to avoid her sister's wedding and partly because grief-work appraisals pay well. She establishes her creed: everything can be measured, nothing is haunted, and people who claim otherwise are grieving, not seeing. Emotional beat: armored competence masking a decade of deliberate self-erasure.

chapters.title: Hollowmere
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. First approach to the house at dusk: it sits wrong on its lot, setback deeper than the deed allows. The Delacorte family—widowed father Marcus, teenage twins Sela and Theo—greet her with desperate politeness. Ivo notes the house smells of pencil shavings and pond water, the exact smell of her childhood. Emotional beat: uncanny familiarity she refuses to name.

chapters.title: Wren
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. On the porch at the end of the first day sits a small figure made of shadow and chalk-dust: Wren, her imaginary friend from age seven, unchanged. He says only, 'You took your time.' Ivo walks to her car, drives two miles, and turns around, telling herself it's to verify a measurement. Emotional beat: the first hairline crack in her disbelief.

chapters.title: Baseline
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. Ivo runs her full survey: laser measure, plumb line, thermal camera. The interior rooms return measurements larger than the exterior footprint allows—by exactly the same margin every time, as if the discrepancy were deliberate, a signature. She logs it as equipment error. Emotional beat: professional denial beginning to feel like effort.

chapters.title: The Delacortes
chapters.summary: Sela Delacorte's POV. Sela watches the surveyor from the stairs and recognizes the way Ivo stares at the hallway—the way Sela's dead mother used to. The twins have a private tally: doors that open onto rooms that shouldn't exist, a fourth place set at dinner no one remembers laying. Emotional beat: a child's terror outpacing an adult's permission to feel it.

chapters.title: What Wren Counts
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. Wren appears in Ivo's rented room, sitting on the dresser like a gargoyle. He explains the house counts who lives in it, and it's been counting the Delacortes wrong—counting four when there should be three, because the dead mother is still on the ledger. 'Ledgers can be corrected,' he says. Emotional beat: dread arriving dressed as arithmetic.

chapters.title: The Previous Appraisal
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV, with archival documents. Ivo finds the 1971 appraisal in county records: the surveyor's notes deteriorate page by page into a child's handwriting, and the final entry reads 'count of five, corrected.' The surveyor, Edith Marsh, was never seen again. Emotional beat: Ivo realizes she is following a paper trail into a mouth.

chapters.title: Sela's Map
chapters.summary: Sela's POV. Sela confronts Ivo with her own hand-drawn map of the house—rooms that appear and disappear, marked in dates. Ivo's measurements match Sela's map exactly. Two skeptics, one child and one adult, recognize each other. Emotional beat: the first alliance, fragile and wordless.

chapters.title: Theo Goes Quiet
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. Theo stops speaking—not traumatized, just economizing, as if words were being deducted from him. Ivo finds him standing in the pantry at 3 a.m., counting under his breath, and when she asks what he's counting he says, 'Me. It's winning.' Emotional beat: protective panic Ivo can no longer file as anything else.

chapters.title: The Wedding I Missed
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV, phone call with her sister Priya. Priya accuses Ivo of hiding inside her work, of having been 'invisible since Dad died.' Ivo, shaken, realizes Wren appeared the year their father vanished from her life—the imaginary friend was a witness to something she chose to forget. Emotional beat: identity cracking along an old fault line.

chapters.title: Edith Marsh's Car
chapters.summary: Ivo and Sela, alternating POV. Following the 1971 notes, they find a rusted sedan in the overgrown back acre, and beneath the floor of the root cellar, a surveyor's stake driven through a child's shoe. The house didn't take Edith; Edith tried to take the house, and the house defended its count. Emotional beat: the rules are real, and they are not merciful.

chapters.title: Correction
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. Wren reveals the mechanism: the house must balance its ledger. If the dead mother is removed from the count, a living resident must be added—or the whole household folds. Marcus, desperate, has already begun leaving offerings, feeding the count without knowing it. Emotional beat: the horror of good intentions compounding the debt.

chapters.title: Marcus's Confession
chapters.summary: Marcus Delacorte's POV. Marcus admits he felt his wife's presence the night she died—she stood at the foot of his bed and asked to stay, and he said yes. He has been saying yes ever since, in small ways, every night. He begs Ivo, the professional, to tell him it's grief. She cannot. Emotional beat: loyalty and truth tearing in opposite directions.

chapters.title: The Count Reaches Five
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. The tally tips: five names on the ledger. The house begins to act—hallways lengthen toward the twins' bedrooms, the front door opens onto the kitchen, and the walls exhale pencil-shaving breath. Ivo's instruments now return her own childhood handwriting. Emotional beat: the countdown made physical, no room left for interpretation.

chapters.title: Run
chapters.summary: Sela's POV. Sela gets Theo out through a window that is briefly a window; Marcus refuses to leave, saying his wife is still in the house. The twins wait at the property line, watching the windows rearrange themselves like a face trying to remember its own expression. Emotional beat: the agony of escape that isn't whole.

chapters.title: What Ivo Forgot
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. Wren shows her the memory she buried: at seven, after her father's disappearance, Ivo asked Wren to make her invisible so nothing could be taken from her again. The house heard. Her entire adult life of self-erasure was the house's first correction, deferred. Emotional beat: devastating reframe—her identity was the debt all along.

chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. Wren lays out the trade: a living name freely given can replace the dead one. Ivo can put her own name on the ledger and walk the Delacortes out—or stay invisible, let the count fall due, and keep the self she's been hiding inside. Emotional beat: the book's thematic fulcrum, justice outside any law but the house's.

chapters.title: Negotiating with the Walls
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. Ivo does what she does best: she surveys. She walks every room, measures every correction, and finds the ledger's loophole—a name can be amended, not just replaced. She begins rewriting the count in her own hand, in her own blood-ink, while the house fights her with shifting geometry. Emotional beat: competence as courage; the skeptic's tools turned into weapons.

chapters.title: The Mother's Name
chapters.summary: Marcus's POV. Marcus, finally understanding, goes to the foot of his bed and says goodbye—releases his wife aloud, by name, with love instead of refusal. Her presence lifts like fog off a pond. The ledger loses its dead weight, and the house shudders, hungry for the balance Ivo has promised. Emotional beat: grief completed at last, and the terrible cost of the delay.

chapters.title: The Count of One
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. The climax: Ivo signs her own name into the ledger as the balancing entry and walks Wren to the front door. The house pulls at her—rooms offering her the invisible life she asked for, warm and safe and never seen. She measures the doorway one last time, steps through it as herself, and the door becomes wall behind her. Emotional beat: triumph and sacrifice fused; visibility chosen at the highest price.

chapters.title: Appraisal Complete
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. Weeks later: the Delacortes' new house measures exactly what it should. Ivo files the Hollowmere appraisal with one line of professional notes and a personal addendum she'll never submit: 'Property is occupied. Property is aware. Do not return.' Theo, recovering, waves at her from the porch of the new house. Emotional beat: quiet aftermath, scar tissue forming.

chapters.title: Seen
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV, closing chapter. At Priya's wedding, Ivo gives a toast, visible, terrified, alive. That night, chalk-dust on her windowsill: not Wren, but a note in a child's hand—'You were always my favorite measurement. —E.M.' Ivo smiles, the right smile this time, and leaves the window open. Emotional beat: identity reclaimed, vigilance kept, horror with a door left ajar.
